The house, inherited from a great-aunt whose name had long since faded from memory, stood as it always had—half in shadow, half in memory, its floorboards creaking softly as if recalling footsteps that had never been hers. Her hoots were not songs but decrees, and when she flew at dusk, the other birds scattered like leaves.

The hills on either side were steep and clothed in a dense, quiet kind of green that seemed to lean inward, listening.

But the day it struck thirteen, I knew there was something wrong—not with the clock, but with me.

It was the only time she ever allowed herself to walk slowly, to let her bare feet imprint the beach like footnotes in a book she had not yet read. The sand was cold here, even in summer, and it reminded her of something—something she had forgotten to remember.
